slides.text: Which of them would you want waiting for you? Answer below.

caption:
Few cultures let the dead walk alone.

In Egypt, Anubis tended the scales where the heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at.
In Greece, Hermes led the shades down, and Charon took the obol at the river.
The Aztecs buried a dog with the dead, to carry them across.
Odin's Valkyries chose the fallen. Yama judged. Azrael waited for the hour.

The Greeks gave Hermes the title: psychopompos, guide of souls.

Which one would you want at your door? Answer below.

The full entry waits in the Forbidden Library: alloccult.com/death-afterlife/death-cults-psychopomps

review_log.summary: Strong hook, accurate core facts and a good Valkyrie and Yama pairing. Not ready to post. Three images miss their subjects. Slide 2 shows Seth and Taweret figures, not a clear Anubis. Slide 5 shows generic Aztec busts with no Mictlan, dog or death imagery. Slide 8 puts a Roman plague scene from Christian legend under an Islam kicker. Slide 3 leaves '24.' orphaned on its own line. The caption overclaims with 'every culture' and 'the Greeks called them psychopomps'.
fixes: slide 2 image: The plate's labelled figures are Seth, Taweret ('Te-oer'), 'Las-an-ho?' and a pantheic bronze. None reads as the jackal-headed Anubis the text describes, and there is no weighing scene.
slide 3 text: 'Homer sings it in Odyssey 24.' is flat and leaves '24.' orphaned on its own line. Odyssey 24 has a far darker, accurate detail to use instead.
slide 5 image: The image is a bust of an Aztec priestess or divinity and a basalt statuette. There is nothing of Mictlan, the dog or death, so it is unrelated to the slide's subject.

slide 8 image: This is Delaunay's Plague in Rome, from Christian Golden Legend imagery: a good angel directs a demon to strike doors. It is a European Christian scene, not Islamic, so it mismatches the Islam / Malak al-Mawt slide.

caption: 'Every culture that buried its dead sent someone to collect them' is a universal claim the archive does not support. 'The Greeks called them psychopomps' misstates the history: psychopompos was a Greek epithet, chiefly of Hermes, and the cross-cultural category is modern scholarly usage. The Anubis line also smooths over his role, since he tends the scales.

review_log.summary: The text is accurate and on-voice throughout, and the caption is clean. Three images fail. Slide 2 is a pun: an etching of Daniel Lambert 'weighing 51 stone' sits under the weighing of the heart. Slides 5 and 8 use unrelated portraits, a Walter Shirlaw self-portrait and the sculptor Desjardins. Replace those three images before posting.
fixes: slide 2 image: Pun and coincidence. The image is an etching of Daniel Lambert 'weighing 51 stone', a famously obese man, placed under the weighing of the heart. It has nothing to do with Anubis and reads as an unintended joke.
slide 5 image: Unrelated image. It is a 19th-century self-portrait of the painter Walter Shirlaw, with no connection to Mictlan, the Aztecs or the Xolo dog.
slide 8 image: Unrelated image. It is a formal portrait engraving of the sculptor Martin Desjardins and has nothing to do with Malak al-Mawt or Azrael.

review_log.summary: Not ready to post. Three images are title-word coincidences rather than the subject: slide 2 shows Daniel Lambert ('weighing'), rendered as an empty frame; slide 5 is a Corot Italian landscape unrelated to Mictlan; slide 8 shows angelfish for the Angel of Death. Slide 2 text overclaims Anubis's role. Anubis tends the scales, while the heart is weighed in Osiris's hall. The rest is accurate, legible and on-voice. The hook is strong and the caption is clean.
fixes: slide 2 image: Image is 'Daniel Lambert, weighing almost forty stone', a pun on 'weighing' with no connection to Egypt. It also renders as an empty picture frame.

slide 2 text: Overclaims. Anubis tends and adjusts the scales, but he does not personally judge the weighing. Thoth records the result, before Osiris. Reword to match the caption's 'tended the scales'.
slide 5 image: Corot's 'Remembrance of Italy' is a European tree landscape. It has nothing to do with Aztec belief or Mictlan.
slide 8 image: Image shows angelfish, a pun on 'angel'. It would undercut the brand's seriousness on a slide about Islam.

review_log.summary: Strong hook and solid Greek and Egyptian slides, but the carousel is not ready. Slide 4 repeats the cover engraving. Slides 5 and 6 show only the placeholder sigil, not their subjects. Slide 8 pairs an Islamic kicker with a Western Christian plague scene after Delaunay. Slide 4 overclaims that Greeks universally buried a coin. Slide 7's kicker names Tibet, but the text and image are Indian. The caption and hashtags are fine.
fixes: slide 4 image: The Boitard etching contains the same two Charon scenes as the cover engraving. It reads as a repeat two swipes in.
slide 4 text: Overclaims. Charon's obol was common, not universal, and the page specifies a coin placed in the mouth or on the eyes.
slide 5 image: Shows only the placeholder sigil, not Mictlan or its death lord. Two blank sigil slides in a row stall the carousel.
slide 6 image: Shows only the placeholder sigil, not the Valkyries.
slide 7 text: The kicker claims Tibet, but the text describes the Vedic Yama and the image is an Indian Punjabi print. The text also needs a source anchor for the claim that he found the path first.
slide 8 image: The image is a Western Christian plague scene after Delaunay, set in Rome. It does not depict the Islamic Angel of Death and misrepresents the tradition named in the kicker.

review_log.summary: Strong hook, sound structure and mostly accurate copy, but four fixes are needed before posting. Slide 4's image is a Gillray political satire of the 'All the Talents' ministry, which is comedic, off-brand and full of caricature nudity. Slide 7 attributes Yama's role as judge to the Rig Veda, but that role comes from later texts. Slides 5 and 6 reuse the same generic sigil, and with slide 8 that makes three identical frames. A relevant image should be tried for each, keeping the sigil on the Islam slide, where aniconic restraint suits the subject. The caption and hashtags are fine.
fixes: slide 4 image: Gillray's 'Charon's Boat, or the Ghosts of All the Talents' (1807) is a political caricature of Grenville's ministry. It is comedic satire rather than an image of the myth, it is crowded with lampooned naked politicians, and it clashes with the brand's voice.
slide 4 text: The facts are accurate. The kicker 'The Ferryman' breaks the 'Culture · Figure' pattern used on every other slide.
slide 5 image: The generic heptagram sigil does not show Mictlan or its dog, and it is repeated on three slides, which makes the carousel feel empty.
slide 6 image: This is the same generic sigil as slides 5 and 8. A Valkyrie engraving or illustration would carry the slide.

slide 7 text: The text overclaims. In Rig Veda 10.14 Yama is the first mortal to die, the finder of the path and king of the dead. His role as judge of the dead comes from later epic and Puranic texts, not the Rig Veda.

review_log.summary: Strong hook, cover and caption. Slide 7 has a factual error: the Rig Veda already calls Yama king (RV 10.14), so only the judge role is later. Four content slides (4, 5, 6, 8) use the generic sigil instead of their subject, which makes the middle of the carousel visually flat. Each gets an image query. Slides 1, 2, 3 and 9 are fine, and the closing card is legible.
fixes: slide 4 image: Generic sigil placeholder; does not show Charon, the ferry or the obol.
slide 5 image: Generic sigil placeholder; nothing of Mictlan, its death lord or the dog.
slide 6 image: Generic sigil placeholder; does not show Valkyries.

slide 7 text: Inaccurate. Rig Veda 10.14 already names Yama king ('King Yama') of the dead; only his role as judge comes in later texts. Also, the explicit 'first of mortals to die' wording is Atharva Veda 18.3.13; the Rig Veda says he found the path for many.
slide 8 image: Generic sigil placeholder; does not show the Angel of Death.

review_log.summary: The text is accurate, tight and on-voice throughout. The Odyssey 24 bats, the Rig Veda Yama, the hedged obol claim and the Mictlan nine levels over four years all check out. Images on slides 1-4, 7 and 9 are relevant, public domain and legible. The weakness is visual: three content slides (5, 6, 8) carry only the generic heptagram fallback, and none shows its subject. Replace them with real archive images before posting. The caption and hashtags are fine.
fixes: slide 5 image: Generic heptagram placeholder; shows nothing of Mictlan, its lord or the Xolo dog. It is also one of three sigil slides, which makes the carousel feel empty.
slide 6 image: Generic heptagram placeholder; does not show Valkyries or Valhalla.
slide 8 image: Generic heptagram placeholder; does not show the Angel of Death.

review_log.summary: Strong, accurate carousel. The cover hook stops the scroll and the cover image is on-subject. Every content slide pairs a relevant public-domain image with historically sound text: Anubis at the weighing of the heart with Ammit; Hermes driving the suitors' shades like bats in Odyssey 24; the obol for Charon, hedged with 'many'; Valkyries and Valhalla; and Yama in Rig Veda 10.14 as the first to find the path of the dead, later the judge. The voice is dark and concise, and nothing is cheesy, banned or misdated. The caption is accurate and on-brand. The closing card is legible.
